genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the central figure works as a repairer of technical objects
she begins by examining the energy stores
she can tell in advance which energy stores will run too hot
she is also drawn to very small drive motors
she opens waterproof casings while sparing the sealing ring
her workroom is cramped and poorly lit
she keeps her screws sorted by size
she welcomes and informs curious passers-by
she refuses to get rid of an object she has not inspected
she machines the parts that cannot be found anywhere
text: You could pass her in the street and never guess what she mends behind that door. Mending broken gadgets is her trade, and the batteries are what she reaches for first: she prises them open, coaxes them patiently back to life, and can tell from the swell of a cell which ones will run hot once they are wired in. Tiny drive motors come next, the kind you have to unpick with fine tweezers to free a bent spindle. Then the casings, above all the sealed ones, which she eases apart without nicking the rubber ring. The workshop is a single cramped room, dim beyond the reach of her lamp, with a bench and drawers of screws graded by size. She is glad to talk shop with anyone who wanders in, and she will not bin a device she has not yet opened. When a part cannot be found, she cuts it herself, filing metal half the evening.

units: the maker claimed a week of use away from the mains
unpacking gives a flattering first impression
the device is described as very light
the display stays readable under harsh light
no noise comes out of the machine during demanding tasks
after long use the shell warms near the hinge
endurance collapses once the wireless link is switched on
a software fix has not removed the lag in typing
the reviewer finds the price excessive for what is delivered
text: The makers promised a portable reader that would hold out a whole week away from the mains. Out of its box the thing does charm you: a matt shell, a hinge that holds firm under the thumb, a weight that barely registers in the hand. Early sessions bear that out. The screen stays readable in glaring light, and the machine keeps quiet even while it grinds through a heavy file. A week on, the shine wears off. The shell warms near the hinge after a long stretch of work, it takes fingerprints, and the endurance we were promised melts away the moment the wireless link goes on. An update has since tidied up part of this, though the keyboard still trails behind the fingers. The verdict, then: a pleasant enough device, roughly finished, asking a great deal more than it hands back. Better to wait and see what the next generation brings.

units: the writer is writing from his workroom
an old sound receiving set stands beside him
the addressee had predicted that the device was beyond saving
a damaged electrical lead cut the sound at the slightest knock
the writer mended the joint by soldering it again
damp had made the wooden case swell
the top would no longer sit in its housing
sanding restored the sliding of the lid
the device now keeps the writer company in the evenings
the writer invites his correspondent to come and see the result
text: I am writing to you from the workshop, the window open on the yard, with the old wireless set sitting at my elbow. You told me it was past saving, and you were nearly right: the lead inside had frayed, so the sound dropped out whenever anyone knocked the bench. I stripped the wire back, soldered the two strands together again, and the crackling stopped there and then. Damp had got into the cabinet as well; the wood had swollen, and the lid would no longer sit down in its grooves. I sanded it down, patiently, until it slid home again the way it always used to. Now the voices fill the room once darkness comes, and I drift off to them without ever reaching for the volume. You see, it took almost nothing in the end. Do come over when you can and hear for yourself how it sings, now that it breathes freely again.

units: the readings of a heat probe become inaccurate
the sensing element is generally not to blame
a deposit of particles on the wall disturbs the conduction of heat
replacing the whole unit is not necessary
cleaning followed by setting against two fixed marks is enough
checking means comparing the values with those of a control instrument
a steady offset can be made up for by the software
an erratic swing reveals a loss of sealing in the casing
the sealing ring must be renewed before readings resume
text: What is going on when a temperature probe stops giving trustworthy readings? The drift seldom starts in the sensing element itself. It comes from dust settling on the membrane, which spoils the flow of heat across it. Does that mean the whole module has to be thrown out? In most cases, no: clean the membrane, then set the instrument against two steady reference points, and the numbers fall into line again. How do you know the work has taken? Stand the probe beside a checking instrument and watch the pair of them over a long stretch. A gap that holds steady is a leftover offset, and software will take care of that. And when the gap wanders about with no pattern to it? The casing has almost certainly lost its seal, letting moisture in among the contacts. Fit a fresh ring before you begin another round of readings.

units: a technical manager questions a skilled worker about the choice of a machine
two devices are weighed against each other
the older device runs without any electrical supply
it is set going by a foot control
the newer device is markedly faster
the newer device stops by itself when something jams
the newer device calls for regular servicing
the older one is mended with rudimentary tools
the two speakers decide to keep both machines
a fresh look at the choice is planned after a season of use
text: The engineer asked the fitter which of the two machines he would sooner see kept on the shop floor. He came down on the older one: mechanical through and through, driven by a foot treadle, and needing no electrical supply at all. She countered that the newer machine works far faster and that it halts of its own accord the instant a piece jams. He granted her the point readily enough, then reminded her that the newer machine has to be serviced to a schedule, whereas the old one comes right again with a spanner and a little patience. Her suggestion was to hold on to the pair of them and bring the powered model in only for the long runs. He agreed, so long as the team learn to handle the older one first. They settled on looking at the whole question afresh once a full season of work in the shop had gone by.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping sounds meant finding a way to inscribe them
the first method cut a groove by means of a vibrating point
that method made it possible to bring a voice back later
the second method rested on magnetising a ribbon coated with grains
magnetising allowed the content to be wiped and written again
the third method turned the signal into a run of separate values
each method changed practices as much as it changed devices
recordings became in turn portable, copyable without loss, then free of any carrier
this change is presented as a series of trade-offs between quality, sturdiness and ease of copying
text: Before sound could travel anywhere, somebody had to work out how to hold it still. The first answer was mechanical: a needle hung from a membrane cut a groove into soft material, and a voice could be carved there and played back afterwards. The second answer was magnetic. A ribbon coated in fine grains held the direction of a field, so what had been laid down could be wiped and written over. The third answer was numerical: the flowing signal was chopped into separate values, stored, then put together again on playback. Every one of these steps altered habits quite as much as it altered the hardware. Recordings could be carried about, then copied with nothing lost, then passed on with no carrier at all. The whole story reads as a long run of bargains struck between fidelity, toughness and ease of copying.

units: sending a message sets off its cutting into very short pieces
each piece carries a marking of the arrival address
the pieces travel first through the air to the nearest relay
obstacles of building are not enough to stop reception by that relay
the pieces carry on through wired links buried or laid under water
their route changes at every node according to crowding
the device at the far end puts the pieces back in the right order
the whole journey takes an extremely short time
a lost piece is asked for again automatically without the user noticing
text: Think for a moment about what happens as soon as you tap send. Your handset chops the message into tiny pieces first, and tags every one of them with a label saying where it has to end up. Off they go through the air to the nearest mast, which manages to pick your handset up even through the walls around you. From there they run along cables, most of them buried under the ground or laid across the seabed, and at every junction they take whichever route is least crowded. They land at last on the handset at the far end, which sorts them back into order and rebuilds your sentence. All of that takes less time than the blink of an eye, however far it has to go. And if a piece goes astray on the way, nothing is lost: your handset asks for it again straight away, and you never notice a thing.

units: the night team took no notice of the stopping of a cabinet fan
the coolness of the room put them off acting at once
the heat probe had been moved the day before because of cabling work
it was reading the temperature of a nearby passage instead of the trapped hot air
no alarm went off despite the building heat
two storage units gave out at the end of the night
the incident cut the electronic mail service for a very wide public
the inquiry puts the failure down to the unrecorded moving of the probe
a written procedure now governs any change of place of a probe
text: It began with a detail the night shift had shrugged off at first: the fan in one of the computer cabinets had gone quiet. The room itself felt cool enough, so nobody saw any reason to act before morning came. The trouble was that the heat probe had been shifted the day before to make room for cabling work, and it was now sampling the air of the corridor next door rather than the still air trapped behind the machines. Warmth built up behind them steadily, and not one alarm sounded. Towards dawn two drives gave out, and with them went the mail service for many thousands of users. The internal report puts the blame not on the hardware but on a probe that had been moved without anyone writing it down. Since then, shifting a sensor calls for a written note and a check carried out the following day.

units: a hand-cranked torch stops working when its generator seizes
it is advised to lay the object on a pale cloth
this precaution keeps the screws from going astray
the four fasteners in the base come out before the two half-shells are parted
the parting must be done gently to spare the catches
the coil turns out to be fouled by a greasy deposit
cleaning is done dry before the shaft bearing is oiled
a lasting squeak comes from the return spring, which has to be tightened again
putting it back together means not driving the screws fully home at once
the light comes back little by little after long turning of the handle
text: The torch you wind by hand tends to end up at the back of a drawer, silent, because the little generator inside it has seized. Here is how to bring it back to life. Lay it down on a pale cloth, so that no screw can slip away unseen. Take out the four screws in the base, then ease the two halves apart slowly, without straining the catches. Inside you will come upon a grey coil, matted with greasy dust that clogs the windings. Brush it clean while everything is still dry, work the shaft free, and put one drop of thin oil on the bearing. If the handle still squeaks, the fault lies in the return spring: unhook it and tighten it up. Close the shells up, start the screws without driving them home, and wind the handle for a good long while. The beam will come back to you, feeble at first, and then steady.

units: those in charge of a water supply have assessed two monitoring systems
both systems are fitted to comparable pipes
the first uses pressure sensors drawn off the main electrical supply
these sensors report through a shielded wired link
the first gives very frequent readings and flags a loss of water quickly
the second rests on standalone sensors closed inside a watertight case
the second sends its data by radio with very low power draw
the second is less precise but spares any digging work
the study recommends the cabled one on sensitive stretches and the standalone one on distant branches
both systems depend on a hydraulic model updated by staff
text: The people who run a water network have just finished weighing up two monitoring rigs fitted to a matching pair of mains. The first works from pressure sensors drawn off the electrical supply and wired back to a central controller through shielded cable; it reports at very short intervals and flags a leak well before the next round of readings. The second uses standalone probes sealed into a watertight case, sending what they gather by radio on very little power. Its resolution is coarser, but putting it in calls for no digging at all. The study comes down in favour of the cabled rig on the stretches that matter most, where a leak runs up a heavy bill. Standalone probes suit the outlying branches rather better. Both share one weakness: they lean on a hydraulic model that staff must update by hand.
